questions.q: The correct order of reactivity towards SN2 is:
questions.explain: SN2 needs room for backside attack, so primary > secondary > tertiary. The reverse order is the SN1 order.

questions.q: Which observation indicates that a substitution has gone by the SN1 mechanism?
options: The rate doubles when the nucleophile concentration is doubled
An optically active substrate gives a largely racemic product, with a rearranged product also formed
The product has completely inverted configuration
The reaction is fastest for CH₃Br and does not occur for tertiary bromides
questions.explain: SN1 passes through a planar carbocation, which is attacked from both faces (racemisation) and can undergo 1,2-shifts. Rate dependence on [Nu⁻], full inversion and CH₃X > 3° are all SN2 features.

questions.q: Which compound undergoes SN1 hydrolysis fastest?
questions.explain: The methoxy group donates electrons by resonance and stabilises the benzyl cation, while nitro destabilises it; a simple primary alkyl chloride forms a poor carbocation.

questions.q: Arrange the four isomeric bromobutanes in decreasing order of SN1 reactivity: n-butyl bromide (I), isobutyl bromide (II), sec-butyl bromide (III), tert-butyl bromide (IV).
questions.explain: SN1 follows carbocation stability, 3° > 2° > 1°; between the two primary bromides, the (CH₃)₂CH– group gives the isobutyl cation more +I stabilisation. For SN2 the order is exactly reversed.
